title: Bharata and the fawn
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: a king leaves everything to remember God, then rescues a fawn
carry: what the mind keeps remembering, it holds at the end
tomorrow: the Gayatri, word by word: so where is its verb?

cards: King Bharata, the Bhagavata says, ruled so well that the land itself was named after him. Then he gave it all up and went to live by a river in the forest, to spend his days remembering the Lord.
One morning a pregnant deer, startled by a lion's roar, leaps the river. Her fawn slips from her into the water, and she dies soon after. Bharata scoops up the fawn.

He feeds it, worries over it, searches for it when it wanders. Slowly his prayers get shorter, and his thoughts of the fawn get longer. When he dies, the fawn is at his side, and it's the fawn he's thinking of.

teach.h: WHAT THE MIND RETURNS TO, IT CARRIES.
teach.b: So, the story says, he's born next as a deer, one that remembers who he was and stays near the sages. Hindus tell it with a warning and a tenderness: what the mind keeps returning to, it carries to the end.
The Bhagavad Gita says whatever one remembers on leaving the body, to that one goes, having always dwelt on it. Always: the end follows the whole life. Now Isha seventeen.
Vayur anilam amritam: breath, to the deathless wind. And this body, ending in ash.

teach.h: BODY TO ASH. KRATO SMARA: MIND, REMEMBER.
teach.b: Then: krato smara, kritam smara. Mind, remember. Remember what was done.
Verse eighteen turns to the fire: agne naya supatha. Agni, lead us by the good path. Many readers, Shankara among them, hear these lines as a prayer at the moment of death.
It's why Hindus give the body to Agni in cremation, and why many families say God's name beside someone who is dying: so the name the mind has practiced all its life is there at the end.
Smarana, remembering, is a daily practice for exactly this.

teach.h: A WEEK OF THE ISHA, IN SIX STORIES.
teach.b: And the week, once more: Shankara in the alley. Gargi's nots. Shvetaketu, proud.
Janaka with a crown. Markandeya in the flood. Nachiketa refusing gold.
One Upanishad, read slowly to its last request.

how: Agne naya supatha is also a Rig Vedic verse to Agni, and some Hindus recite it at the fire; at a deathbed many families chant God's name or play it softly, and the body is given to Agni in cremation.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha's rules for funeral rites
reading the Isha's final summary of every verse
reading the Isha's own words, through to its last request

games.q: the king, the fawn and the last verses — tap the pairs.
p: the king who left all, then loved a fawn
Agni, lead us by the good path

s: the Isha ends with a summary of its teaching
it ends with a request: Agni, lead us by the good path.
in the Bhagavata, Bharata's last thoughts were of his fawn
and he was born next as a deer, one that remembered.
the Gita says only your final second counts, however you lived
whatever one has always dwelt on: the end follows the habit of a life.

games.q: a friend's grandfather is dying, and her family chants God's name by his bed. she asks you why. by the Gita and the Isha's last verses, what's the gentlest true answer?
o: so the name he's practiced all his life is with him at the end: krato smara.
because only the last word decides everything, no matter how he lived.
it's just old habit; it doesn't mean anything.
games.why: the Gita says what one has always dwelt on, one goes to; the Isha's dying prayer says mind, remember. the chanting keeps the lifelong name close.

practice: Count back through today on your fingers: one thing you did this morning, one at midday, one just now. Let each come back plainly, without judging it: smara, remember what was done.
If you pray, end with the name your family says, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Om, softly, three times. If not, end with one thing you'd want to remember. Then rest the hands.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, to its last line: krato smara, mind, remember, and agne naya supatha, Agni, lead us by the good path.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: smara, remember, from Isha 17's krato smara; smarana, remembering God, is a daily practice.

carryVoice: Your line: what the mind keeps remembering, it holds at the end. That's the Isha, start to finish.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 17 (vayur anilam amritam athedam bhasmantam shariram; om krato smara kritam smara)
Isha Upanishad 18 (agne naya supatha raye asman vishvani deva vayunani vidvan; yuyodhy asmaj juhuranam eno; bhuyishtham te nama-uktim vidhema)
Bhagavata Purana 5.7–5.8 (Bharata renounces the kingdom; the doe, the fawn in the river, his attachment, his last thought, his birth as a deer)
Bhagavad Gita 8.6 (yam yam vapi smaran bhavam tyajaty ante kalevaram; tam tam evaiti kaunteya sada tad-bhava-bhavitah)
Shankara, commentary on Isha Upanishad 15–18 (the closing verses as the prayer of one at the time of death)
